# Results

This section shows both a generated figure (produced by a Python code
cell, which is why the project uses `uv`) and a hand-written table.

```{python}
#| label: fig-valence
#| fig-cap: "Classifier comparison for the target variable valence (example)."
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 4.2
#| fig-height: 2.6
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

models = ["RF (snorm)", "XGB (raw)", "XGB (snorm)", "NN (snorm)", "RF (raw)", "NN (raw)"]
f1 = [0.42, 0.39, 0.39, 0.36, 0.35, 0.34]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(range(len(models)), f1)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(models)))
ax.set_xticklabels(models, rotation=45, ha="right", fontsize=7)
ax.set_ylabel("f1 macro")
ax.set_ylim(0, 0.6)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

As shown in @fig-valence, Random Forest on session-normalized features
performed best. If you prefer not to run code, delete the cell above and
use a static image instead (see `04-method.qmd`).

## Model Performance

: Model performance by target variable. Table captions carry a bold
"Table N." label and no terminal punctuation {#tbl-perf}

| Target   | Best model            | Accuracy | f1 macro |
|----------|-----------------------|:--------:|:--------:|
| Valence  | RandomForest (snorm)  |  36–43%  |   0.42   |
| Arousal  | NeuralNet (snorm)     |  32–37%  |   0.36   |
| Emotion  | RandomForest (raw)    |   42%    |   0.21   |

@tbl-perf summarizes the best combination per target variable.
